subject: Culture
title: Aid Politics
description: A micro-lesson that makes Aid Politics usable.

hook.text: US food aid once legally had to be grown in America and shipped on American vessels. Help came with strings.

buildup.text: Food aid can flood local markets, destroying the farmers it's supposed to help.

discovery.text: Economist Amartya Sen showed famines rarely come from food shortage—they come from power imbalances.

twist.text: Some countries refuse foreign food aid to protect national pride. North Korea has done this repeatedly.

climax.text: Giving food sounds simple and pure. In practice, it's tangled with politics, markets, and pride.

punchline.text: Even charity comes with a cost.

quiz.question: What did economist Amartya Sen argue about famines?
options: They result from power imbalances, not just food shortage

details.summary: Food aid is never purely charitable — it serves diplomatic, economic, and political agendas alongside humanitarian ones. US food aid has historically required using American-grown grain shipped on American vessels, benefiting American farmers and shippers while often undermining local food markets.
details.whyItMatters: Understanding food aid politics prevents naive assumptions about charity. Aid that serves donor interests at the expense of recipient self-sufficiency can cause more harm than hunger itself.
takeaways: US food aid laws historically required buying American grain
Food aid can crash local markets and displace local farmers
Cash-based aid is more efficient but faces political opposition

faq.question: How can food aid be harmful?
faq.answer: Dumping free food into a local market crashes prices, driving local farmers out of business. This creates long-term dependency on aid. Shipping food from donor countries is slower and more expensive than buying locally.

faq.question: What is the alternative to food aid?
faq.answer: Cash transfers and vouchers allow recipients to buy food locally, supporting local markets and farmers. Local and regional food procurement is faster and cheaper than transatlantic shipping. Building agricultural capacity (seeds, tools, training) creates long-term food security.
